If the business is to be handled properly, there must be some change. I wrote the minister in regard to the congestion in the temporary Toronto customs house, where people who are doing business have to waste a great deal of their time standing in line. The Government have a rented custom building in Toronto, and if they keep on the way they are going, they will have a tent next for their custom house. sary repairs throughout Ontario; the money was available but, for some reason or other, it has not been spent. The Toronto post office and custom house come under this item for repairs. I am rather startled, however, at the general hue and cry which comes to us to-night from the great province of Ontario. I have been sitting in this House for

They may have been in the secrets of this chamber with the then Prime Minister; but I invite him to search the pages of Hansard when the estimates of his ministers were going through, to find any complaints, for instance, from hon. members for Toronto. It is true that the people of that city had but third or fourth or fifth-rate men compared with what they have been sending us lately; but nevertheless those men thought that they were doing the best they could, and yet we heard nothing about the post office. I believe Toronto was on the map during the last ten or fifteen years; at all events, it was on the map while the hon. gentleman (Mr. Church) who represents that city, was mayor. He was on the map during those years; he is on the map now, and it is too bad if the city was so badly neglected that, to-day, when there is a change of government for only three or four months or less, the deplorable condition of things, which hon. members for Toronto present, and present truthfully, 
exists in that city. I am surprised that they should have put up with this, but they have put up with it until they are beginning really and thoroughly to understand that they are being neglected in the way that they are. I am sorry that the affairs of the province of Ontario, in Hamilton, in Galt, in Toronto itself and all around, have been so neglected; and I think it is only fair that I should mention that, if the government of the right hon. gentleman (Mr. Meighen) who now leads the Opposition, was such a good government as hon. gentlemen used to say it was, and if it was doing its duty to the people of Toronto in public matters, it is surprising that, after it has been out of power only for three or four months, conditions which have been put forward to-night should be found to exist. There is only one way in which that could have occurred. Ten years ago when the Laurier government went out of power, we had no such complaints. Although we had, in those days of the Laurier regime, a very vigorous opposition from Ontario, we heard very little about those things, I cannot recall any particular complaints; and for that reason and because that vigorous opposition did not find much fault, I can only explain the matter in one way, that a fair distribution of public money was being made and that public buildings were being kept in excellent repair. Ten years of the administration of hon. gentlemen opposite have passed by, and the condition we find is as it has been described. I would be sorry to think, for one moment, that hon. gentlemen would give a description of the condition in which that province is left other than what it is. If it is what they represent it to be, there is only one story, and that is that their friends, in whom they had such confidence and in whose hands they left the administration of this country and would have continued to leave it, have neglected them to the extent they have. It is hardly fair that the present Minister of Public Works (Mr. King), who is here but a few weeks, who is a stranger to his department, who is making the most of the legacy that has been handed down to him by the outgoing Minister of Public Works of the Tory administration, should be catechised unduly. It is proper to ask questions; but it is hardly fair that with bell, book and candle he should be criticised and held responsible for conditions that have been handed down to him and that he has just begun to acquaint himself with.

I am not trying to be critical of anyone, but I think it is only fair to point out to the committee and to the country that the present ministers who are getting along as best they can with these estimates are taking up the burden that was laid down but a few days ago by their predecessors in office, who of necessity were better acquainted with their departments than the present ministers can be expected to be after having been in control for only a few months. It is well to point out that such improvements are necessary, but I do not think that hon. gentlemen can afford to give themselves such airs and be so critical and fault-finding when they reflect for a moment that this is a legacy which they themselves have handed down to the present Government.

Mr. Chairman, the
committee could not help but lament while listening to the masterly speech of the Solicitor General that a gentleman of his talents should now be cribbed, cabined and confined within the comparatively inactive environment of the Solicitor General's office. It is too bad that a large department demanding the application of business talents is not under his charge.
I will try first to extract the point he intended to make and that perhaps somewhere is drowned in the deluge of his words. He says: If there is a dearth of public buildings in Ontario the fault is with the late government, and you should have made bitter complaints during the tenure of office of the late government, rather than address those complaints to the novice ears of the present Minister of Public Works (Mr. King), who really, so the Solicitor General intimates, knows nothing about the department. That apparently is the point the Solicitor General tries to make. Yes, there is a dearth of public buildings in Ontario, a dearth for which the late government holds itself coresponsible. But what the Solicitor General forgets and has too often forgotten in recent years is that the late government carried this country through a war, that the late government turned the energy of the nation into the war, that the late government devoted the resources of the country to the war, and that consequently public works throughout that period had to wait. We said to our members, and they accepted our words, that until we got through the war, and the after effects of the war, we could not go on with the construction of further public works unless
imperatively necessary and we did not, as evidenced by the words of the Minister of Public Works to-night, as respecting one item after another, he tells us only a small amount was asked for of which only a trifling portion was spent. That is the actual fact, and members accordingly did not press unreasonably for public improvements. We had to go along with just as little expenditure on public works as possible, having in mind the major necessities of the nation, and that we did so is a matter for general congratulation. That was the position we took on the floor of Parliament, and hon. members and the country accepted our answer, because it was a good answer. That is the reason why these needs face us to-day. We have needs, it is true. We do not want to press any more than do hon. members for expenditure beyond the financial resources of the country. I do not think we should go on with large public expenditures-none except those which are quite unavoidable. But I cannot help recaling that though I went through province after province, and made no promise of public expenditure for the sake of getting a single vote, made, for example, in Prince Edward Island, near the minister's home, a frank statement that we would not claim to be able now to go on with the widening of the railway gauge in that island, I was followed by his leader, who criticised me from the stump throughout the Island because I failed to make a promise to spend millions of dollars on that enterprise. Possibly the recklessness of his leader's promises and intimations counts in some degree for a measure of the support that is found in his party in the House now; I do not doubt that it does; but upon their fulfilment depends what little there is left of the reputation of the Government, and there will be some penalty to pay in respect of their nonfulfilment, just as in recent days we have witnessed the penalty that the Government has had to pay in respect to other pledges that they have abandoned.

Perhaps the Solicitor
General takes his politics and his religion too seriously. He is, I understand, a doctor; he is a D.D., anyway-I do not know whether a Doctor of Divinity or not. I think the hon. gentleman might be better employed in helping his young colleague to explain this item. I wish to give the Minister of Public Works every support, and it may be that he is not getting the support that he should receive. But the

Solicitor General must understand that there are no politics in this so far as Toronto is concerned. I have ah'eady laid it down very clearly that what we want is a proper post office and custom house to efficiently take care of the great volume of business there. These public utilities should be considered from the commercial aspect only. Away back when Sir Wilfrid Laurier was in power the then member for South Toronto, Mr. Claude Macdonell, year in and year out called the attention of the government of the day to the deplorable state of affairs of the Toronto postoffice and customs house. The government tore down the old customs house, but no new accommodation has yet been provided. If they did not intend to build a new customs house, adequate to the present day needs of the city, why did they tear down the old building? I complained for seven years about these things to the late government. It is the duty of the government to give proper administration of the post-offices. There should be a reduction in the rate on drop letters. Although $5,000,000 is taken out of the pockets of the citizens of Toronto, they are still charged two cents for drop letters. The rate should go back to one cent for drop letters. It is not creditable to public ownership that the administration of our post-offices and customs houses either in Montreal, Toronto, Winnipeg or any other city should be so inadequaate that the public suffer through the lack of proper plant or service. Only a few days ago the Postmaster General of the United States said that the time had come when the public should be given the best accommodation in the shape of post-offices and customs houses. And the public are entitled to it. Why should the people have to line up at the customs house in Toronto or any other city to wait as long as seventy-five minutes before they get up to the wicket? Why should politics be brought into this matter? I would make the same complaint in regard to Montreal, or any other post-office in the minister's own riding. I may be a little unfair to the Minister of Public Works in asking him about post-offices and customs houses which are not under his department, but this is the only opportunity we get under the rules of the House to bring the matter up. When the Government derives $5,000,000 revenue from Toronto's postoffice, they should certainly provide a proper plant for the accommodation of the public. Those who have to go to the 
customs house are losing thousands of dollars every day owing to the grossly inadequate accommodation. I do not care whether a Liberal government, a Conservative or even a U.F.O. government be in power, the people are entitled to proper post-office and customs house accommodation. I venture to say that a great deal more revenue would be derived from the Toronto post office if proper accommodation were provided, and from fifteen to twenty per cent more revenue would be received from a customs house in which the public could get proper service. Adequate accommodation should be provided, whether it be in Toronto, Montreal, Vancouver or any other of our cities. I hope during the recess the Minister of Public Works, the Postmaster General and the Minister of Finance will look into these things and give the people some relief. They have been clamouring for this for ten or twelve years, but nothing has been done. The Solicitor General would be better advised if he would preach fewer sermons and give us more information; there is plenty of time for sermons on Sunday. There is one minister on the treasury benches who is a pulpit orator and takes his turn on Sunday; the next to do that, I suppose, will be the hon. Solicitor General.
How is this $95,000 for improvements, repairs, etc., to be distributed through Ontario?
I am not able to give that information. It is to meet the requirements as they come up throughout the year.

In view of the fact that Toronto and suburbs have postal receipts equal to those of Montreal or any twenty other cities in Quebec, is it possible to say how much of the $95,000 will be devoted to the Toronto district?
No; it will depend on the requirements of that district.

The minister's answer to me a few minutes ago with respect to that revote at ,St. Catharines was not, in my estimation, a very satisfactory one. Would he, when his estimates come up again, give us some information with regard to that revote?
Yes.

The Solicitor General twitted us with not having last year pressed the then government to make improvements in our respective counties. The Solicitor General himself was never back-

ward in coming to the committee and pressing very hard for whatever was wanted by Nova Scotia.

That is why I expected hon. members to have the courage of their convictions when they believed things were needed in Ontario, and to put their case before the House. When no such complaints were made, I had reason to suppose that everything was all right. But when it was a Tory government and there was Tory neglect, everything was regarded forgivingly and nothing was said. The ex-Prime Minister told us tonight that they could not spend any more money for these purposes. Up to the sixth of December, any requests for these things were met by the answer that all the money had been used and was being used for war and demobilization purposes, but what a tremendous change took place following the election! The first week in the House under the new administration that excuse was forgotten; it was no longer good. Well, if the lack of money on account of war expenditure was a good answer to these requests while the war was on and for the three years following the war, surely it ought to be an answer to be given by this Government, at least until it has an opportunity of settling the bills left unpaid and unprovided for by the late administration. These are the reasons I give for expecting hon. gentlemen to be reasonable in their criticism.

I am sure we are glad to have the second instalment of the hon. gentleman's lecture. But I do not think the minister has been unfairly treated; he has asked for no quarter and has made no complaint. I know I have been courteous in my remarks, and I do not think the lecture of the hon. gentleman is called for. But I would say this in reply to his remarks: we are getting further from the war every day, and as the business of the post offices increases, as exemplified by Toronto, for instance, these necessities become more pressing. The situation in Ed-mundston is due to a large increase in the activities of the commercial life of the community, and it is absolutely necessary that postal facilities be provided there. It is for that reason, and not because there has. been a change of administration, that gentlemen on this side are doing their duty in directing the minister's attention to these circumstances. There is no necessity, therefore, for the Solicitor General
rising up in his righteousness and giving us a lecture on propriety.

At the last election the Liberal candidates in Toronto district promised a new post office and customs house for Toronto if their party was returned; the public were assured that they would not have to suffer long. I hope that during the recess a survey of the situation will be made; there have been a hundred surveys in the past fifteen years.
I hope something will be done to do away with the condition under which the people have to transact their business owing to congestion. The custom work will be transacted next out on the sidewalk if it continues-because that is what it is coming to. The same state of affairs prevails in Hamilton; there is positive congestion, and I do not see how they get on with the business. I hope the Government will look into these things in the interests of efficiency and with a view of retaining the confidence of the people in these public services.

speechtext: I wish to say a few words in reply to the remarks of the hon. Solicitor General (Mr. McKenzie) . I was somewhat surprised at the argument he put up to-night. If he lived in Hamilton as I do and saw the treatment which has been meted out to that city for the past few years, he would tell a different story. Some years ago the old buildings were torn down, two or three hundred thousand dollars spent on the purchase of land and an appropriation of $300,000 or $400,000 put in the estimates for a new post office building. In 1914 the war came on and the matter was allowed to stand. I do not blame the government for that; they had their hands full, and I do not think anybody could find fault with the way they acquitted themselves. But three years have passed since the conclusion of the war, and for the last six or seven years we in Hamilton have not received a cent of money for improvements of any kind. Hamilton has not been fairly treated, particularly in view of the revenue it produces, and I think it is about time we got some money for the buildings that we so badly need.
Last year the total vote under this item was $1,012,267. I understood the minister to say that the sum of $700,000, in round numbers, was spent last year. Is that correct?

The public business is
greatly expanding in Ottawa, and in my opinion the individual buildings which the Government is buying cannot adequately accommodate the public service. I would like to emphasize the remarks of the previous speaker as to the small vote for public buildings for the province of Saskatchewan. The name Saskatchewan is of Indian origin but the people out there are not all Indians, nor does the land1 consist of desert or Indian reserves either. In line with my hon. friend who preceded me, I maintain that this vote is the smallest appropriation made for any province. The apportionment of public money for Nova Scotia would look to be smaller but if you combine the vote for Nova Scotia of $19,600, the vote of $48,500 for New Brunswick, and the vote of $38,000 for the maritime provinces generally, it will be seen that the average for each of three maritime provinces is over $35,000. Our province of Saskatchewan

is a real large block of land and the population is 200,000 larger than that of either Manitoba or Alberta. I would like also to bring to the attention of the minister the fact that in the town in which I have the honour to live the post office is housed in a small rented shack, and I was informed by the postmaster that he is compelled to move, as the Bank of Commerce which owns the building, is going to haul it away out on the prairies in order that risk of Are may be eliminated. asked for a return showing the amount of rental paid by this Government for public buildings in the various parts of the city of Calgary, but that report has not come to hand. I have heard a good
deal this evening about post offices. I was not asked to get much when I came down here. I was merely asked to gat four post offices, but I am not asking that 'to-night. If there is a place in British Columbia which needs a post office it is Kamloops. We need a building from several standpoints. We have in Kamloops no land or no forestry office accommodation, no telephone office, and several other branches of the Dominion government need accommodation. We should have a post office building there. Money was voted for it some years ago, and I do not see why that money should not be voted again, and, at least, a start made on it. The present post office is a menace to public health. It has been condemned twice by the health inspector of that district. Kamloops is in a central location. It is a distributing point for the North Thompson, for the southern portion of that district and for both east and west, and they have no facilities there for such business. I think it is up to the present minister to take action, and I would like to know what he intends doing with regard to the Kamloops post office.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I think, on the question of buildings generally, I ought, in fairness to my colleague the Minister of Public Works (Mr. King), to take more than a fair share of the responsibility. He is a kindly disposed new member, and I believe he would like to yield to the many requests made for new buildings; but ever since he came here, indeed, almost before he came, I have been preaching to him, warning him against putting into the estimates items for new public buildings. If there is anything in which we can afford to economize this year, it is along that line. I am not referring to any particular building; but I have taken the responsibility of urging all my colleagues along certain lines of economy, and particularly I have asked the Minister of Public Works to resist the applications, many and urgent, for the construction of new public buildings. If that is a bad policy, do not blame the Minister of Public Works entirely for it. I am largely responsible for it.
There is a small item of $1,000 odd for taxes. How does that item arise? Is this not government property?

I am advised that this is an old post office property which the Government rents, and this is an item that has been appearing in the estimates for years. I thought probably it was a local improvement tax. I know there are local improvement taxes which the Government have from time to time, consented to pay in the province.
This is a local improvement tax, I understand?
It is a general tax.
The Crown is not supposed to be taxed for general purposes.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: The building is rented to people for stores.

In Ontario, and in,
perhaps, a number of other provinces, cer-

tain local taxes appear in the larger cities and towns and are imposed upon the principle of so much per front foot. We have, in a number of western Ontario cities, under the authority of our municipal law a tax known as the garbage tax. This is assessed on all the streets of the cities and towns; but when you come to government property, the Government refuses to pay the tax, and I think the refusal is very improper. This tax amounts to a good deal in some of our smaller cities, and complaints have been made in St. Thomas, Galt, Kitchener, Guelph, Stratford anu other places. A city council, for instance, divides up the tax over the different lots on the main street, and everybody on that street is taxed so much per front foot for the collection of garbage. When you come to government property, the waste paper and ashes are thrown out and the city garbage man takes them away; but when the bill comes in, the Government has made it a rule to refuse payment. The Government will pay for local improvement, for city water; but when the question is one of collection of garbage, it makes a distinction and refuses payment. This is most unfair; it means that people who are on a street on which there is government property-and sometimes the government property covers a large block *-have to pay so much more than they should have by reason of the refusal of the Government to pay this tax. The minister should take this matter into serious consideration.
Is that a new tax? When was the law put into force?

We have had it in Oi>
tario for some years.
Why did the old government not fix the matter?

Payment has always
been refused.

It will be news for members from New Brunswick to learn that Crown property in the Dominion pays any taxes at all. At all events, I never heard of any in the province of New Brunswick paying any local improvement taxes.
This is a general tax.

I understood the minister to say that this Crown property in Ontario paid some local improvement tax. I venture to say that the Dominion Government own half a million dollars worth of

Supply-Public Works
property in my city, and it has not paid one dollar of municipal taxation or local improvement taxes or anything else from the beginning of. time. If the Government property pays taxes in Ontario, then I think the Dominion government should, in' all fairness and justice, contribute something towards the municipal burden of keeping up sidewalks in front of its property. It does not even do that in New Brunswick. To what extent is that practice prevalent?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
As I understand the
garbage tax in Ontario, the Government has refused to pay the garbage tax which was very high on its large blocks; but it gets no service from the municipal garbage collector. It looks after the collection of garbage and pays for that. Consequently, it pays no taxes when it does the work.
As regards Government property, the Government is not a landlord; it is not going into the landlord business. When it has property which it leases to some other person, as that other person, if he were on other property, would pay taxes, the Government, under those circumstances, acts like any other landlord and pays the taxes. When, however, the property is used by the Government for Government purposes, it does not pay taxes.

In reference to the post
office situation, if there is anything in the way of precedent in the matter of getting your order in early or of having some justification for your claim, I wish to state that Prince Rupert has been on the map for fifteen years, and it very urgently requires a post office. We have heard a good deal of criticism to-night against the minister for his failure to provide post offices. When the proper time comes, we shall be on deck with our demand for a post office; but I wish to pay a little tribute to the minister. We have had, in Prince Rupert, under the system started some years ago, a very extravagant system of rentals. We have had in that city a federal building housing the post office and the customs department, and various other buildings, for which the Government has paid an annual rental of $11,100 a year. The minister, I understand, has a proposition before him to remove these offices to other premises at a rental of $6,540 a year, and that, I think, is a step in the right direction. The Government is practising economy; it is practising economy in the right direction as regards Prince Rupert. We approve that at present; but when the proper time arrives,
Prince Rupert will be on deck for a post office of its own.

I was much interested in a statement made by the Minister of Militia (Mr. Graham) that, if the Government owns property and rents it to someone else, it invariably pays the tax. The matter has not worked out in that way in my province. As regards soldier settlement farms, farms that have been salvaged from the original settler by the Government and rented to a private individual, the Government is possibly getting a larger revenue from the private farmer than from the soldier settler, and yet it has refused to pay the taxes, even the school tax. This is crippling quite badly school districts in my immediate part of New Brunswick. Perhaps I may be out of order; and if I am, I presume the proper time to discuss this matter will be when the committee's report on Soldiers Civil Re-establishment is before the House. I want however an opportunity of hearing the minister's statement, in regard to the Government paying taxes, and then I shall be pleased to follow it up to see that we get some of these taxes.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: It should be understood by all members that the Minister of Public Works is not responsible for the erection of buildings. Consequently, criticism should be directed against all the rest of us in the other departments for whom the Public Works erects buildings or rents them, because we really are responsible, and the Public Works Department is merely the agent for providing us with that accommodation.

I wish to add my little wail to the complaints that have already gone up in connection with post offices. I will spare the minister getting on his feet to give us the usual excuse, for the department has already turned down my request for the only post office I wanted, the claims for which were so great as to make the claims of Kamloops, Prince Rupert, Victoria and Vancouver shrink into absolute insignificance. I will not weary the committee with details, because I am sure they will take my word for it. I was going to suggest, in view of the statement made by the Minister of Finance, that he with the Minister of Public Works should form a roster, so to speak, and begin it to-night, of those post offices in British Columbia which were to get attention next year, and in order to prevent any disagreement among hon. members I would suggest that the list

Supply-Public Works

be made alphabetical in its character; the post office I want is Courtney.
I was somewhat struck by the modest violet-like innocence of my friends from Vancouver and Victoria when they sought to criticize this vote and, like Oliver Twist, asked for more. I find some $59,000 in this vote, every cent of which will be spent in the constituencies of Victoria and Vancouver from which my hon. friends come. I would remind the Government and particularly the Minister of Public Works, that there are places in British Columbia outside the confines of those municipalities, incredible as it may appear from looking at the public accounts of the last five or six years. I am almost compelled to think that the right hon. leader of the Opposition is a man of far vision and sympathetic touch, for I heard him to-night in the House, unsolicited by anybody from British Columbia, tell one of the Cabinet ministers that in his opinion British Columbia always got the cold shoulder from this Government-an opinion which I very heartily share in, as I think do some other members. I hope the Government will take that into consideration when some of the other public works estimates come down, of a more important character perhaps. I wished to refer to another item but I have forgotten it. I do not suppose it will materially advance the interests of the post office, and probably the House will be glad to be spared any details.

I should like to tell the hon. gentleman who has just taken his seat that I did not criticize the vote for Victoria. I may have thought a little about it, but I did not say anything. All I wanted was some information about how the money was to he spent.

Item agreed to.
Progress reported.
